concept.name: Par value
concept.definition: The principal amount of a bond or note that the issuer promises to repay at maturity, and the base on which coupon interest is calculated; the bond trades at a premium, at par, or at a discount depending on whether its price is above, equal to, or below this amount.
concept.intuition: Par value is the loan amount printed on the bond: whatever the market price does day to day, par is what comes back at the end (absent default).
concept.mechanics: Coupon payments equal par value x coupon rate (split into periodic installments, typically semiannual). At issuance or in the secondary market, price relative to par reflects the relationship between the coupon rate and the prevailing yield: price < par when yield > coupon, and vice versa.
concept.formula: Periodic coupon payment = par value x coupon rate / number of payments per year.
concept.failure_modes: Par value is repaid only if held to maturity and the issuer performs: default or selling early means the investor realizes the market price or recovery value, not par.
concept.misconceptions: Par value is not the bond's market value and not a floor on its price; bonds routinely trade above or below par as rates and credit conditions move.
concept.example: A $1,000-par Treasury note with a 1.75% coupon pays $8.75 every six months and returns the $1,000 par at maturity; it was priced at 98.34 (below par) when its auction yield exceeded the coupon rate.
